title: Americans broadly agree corruption exists and recognize public-power abuses, while partisan identity redirects blame and judgment
source_unit: University of Massachusetts Amherst Poll, September 2026 national public-opinion poll on federal corruption, presidential conduct, national direction, and economic perceptions
geography: United States; adults nationally with party, ideology, demographic, and economic comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed; margin of error plus or minus 3.5 percentage points

at_least_some_corruption.unit: percent saying at least some corruption exists in the federal government

great_deal_corruption.unit: percent saying a great deal of corruption exists

presidency_most_corrupt.unit: percent ranking the presidency as the most corrupt of four federal institutions

wrong_track.unit: percent saying the country is on the wrong track; 20% say right direction

observations.method: UMass Amherst national poll fielded August 21-26, 2026; respondents were matched to an ACS-based sampling frame, propensity-weighted, and raked on presidential vote choice and demographic variables.
observations.uncertainty: These are perceptions, not verified corruption incidents, legal findings, or institutional-performance measures; the poll is cross-sectional and the wrong-track question does not identify causes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with party, ideology, age, race, education, income, and vote-choice comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-universal belief that some corruption exists may express generalized distrust or a broad definition of corruption rather than agreement about specific misconduct; wrong-track judgments can reflect prices, policy, identity, or partisan evaluation.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed; institution-ranking question asks respondents to rank four federal institutions

democrats_presidency_most_corrupt.unit: percent of Democrats ranking the presidency most corrupt

republicans_presidency_most_corrupt.unit: percent of Republicans ranking the presidency most corrupt

republicans_bureaucracy_most_corrupt.unit: percent of Republicans ranking the federal bureaucracy most corrupt

republicans_congress_most_corrupt.unit: percent of Republicans ranking Congress most corrupt

observations.method: UMass poll subgroup comparison using party identification; respondents ranked the president, Congress, Supreme Court, and federal bureaucracy from most to least corrupt.
observations.uncertainty: The partisan differences are associations, not evidence that party identity causes corruption judgments; ranking forces relative choices among institutions and may be sensitive to current officeholders and news context.
observations.subgroup: Democratic and Republican respondents in the August 2026 national poll.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partisan disagreement over institutional location can coexist with cross-party agreement that specific conduct is corrupt; disagreement over the villain is not the same as disagreement over every norm.

observations.period: August 2026; shared standards for public-power abuse

investigation_for_trading_votes.unit: percent of both Democrats and Republicans wanting an investigation when officials trade votes for campaign contributions

president_should_not_profit.unit: percent saying a sitting president should not profit from business ventures potentially affected by administration policy

do_not_trust_avoid_family_business_benef.unit: percent lacking trust that President Trump will avoid using office to benefit his family's business interests

lack_confidence_public_interest.unit: percent lacking confidence in the president's ability to make decisions serving the public interest

observations.method: UMass poll questions about corruption standards and presidential conduct; response options distinguish perceived corruption, investigation preferences, and trust in presidential conduct.
observations.uncertainty: The poll measures stated judgments and trust, not observed enforcement, ethics investigations, legal liability, or subsequent behavior; question wording and current political events may shape responses.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with partisan comparisons reported for selected items.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared standards about self-dealing or vote trading can coexist with partisan double standards about identical actions by presidents of different parties; support for investigation does not guarantee institutional follow-through.

observations.period: October 2024-August 2026; household price perception and political attribution

denominator.unit: poll respondents reporting that at least one listed good or service increased in price, for responsibility question; broader economic ratings use N=1,000

national_economy_fair_or_poor.unit: percent rating the national economy fair or poor in August 2026

own_economy_fair_or_poor.unit: percent rating their own economic situation fair or poor in August 2026

grocery_prices_increased.unit: percent saying grocery prices increased in recent months

utilities_increased.unit: percent saying utility prices increased in recent months

blame_president_for_price_rise.unit: percent of conditional respondents assigning most responsibility to President Trump

observations.method: UMass repeated national poll measures from October 2024 through August 2026, using separate national and own-economic ratings, perceived price-change questions, and a conditional responsibility question.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived price changes and attribution are not price-index or causal-incidence estimates; the responsibility denominator excludes respondents who did not report an increase and the poll does not measure actual household spending or hardship.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally; conditional price-responsibility universe where specified.
observations.counterinterpretation: Households can perceive price pressure while having different actual inflation exposure, income buffers, or coping routes; attributing prices to a president is a political judgment, not a causal estimate.

boundary: This record adds a public-power and attribution layer: Americans broadly perceive federal corruption and price pressure, share some standards for public abuse, but divide sharply over which institution is responsible and how identical conduct should be judged. It does not establish actual corruption, legal violations, causal responsibility for prices, enforcement, institutional remedy, or later political behavior.
